notes: \cpara{The question mark is warranted. David Wheeler, who looked for the source of this example, writes that ``Aristotle did not say anything like this example''; the earliest printing found there is John Stuart Mill's \textsc{A System of Logic} (1843), in the chapter that makes this post's objection (see the note on ``You could reason, perhaps'').}

\cpara{The parable. The student's last move is valid under the student's own definition: if mortality is part of ``man,'' a Socrates who does not die is not a man. The joke is that the certainty costs nothing because it predicts nothing.}
\cpara{States the thesis in one sentence. The linked page is a webcomic whose content I could not see.}

\cpara{The first horn: treat ``all humans are mortal'' as a record of observed cases, and predict from them. This is John Stuart Mill's account of the syllogism, with the same example. Mill granted that ``in every syllogism, considered as an argument to prove the conclusion, there is a petitio principii,'' and answered that ``All inference is from particulars to particulars'' (\textsc{A System of Logic}, Book II, chapter 3). The post does not mention Mill; his account supports it.}

\cpara{The second horn: mortality is part of the definition. The attribution has a basis. Porphyry, a Neoplatonist of the third century AD who wrote in Greek, made ``rational and mortal'' the differences ``constitutive of man,'' and his definition, \mbox{``animal rationale mortale,''} was adopted by medieval logicians (Owen's translation of the \textsc{Isagoge}, text and note 17).}

\cpara{The dilemma's conclusion: on the definitional view, you must see Socrates die before you can call him human. Mill made the same reply to the definitional view in 1843: ``If the word man connoted mortality \ldots\ we might, undoubtedly, evolve the conclusion from the minor alone, because the minor would have already asserted it.'' Mill held that the word ``does not connote mortality.''}
\cpara{An aside that extends the point from this definition to any observation: even seeing him die gives no certainty.}

\cpara{The point here is the textbook distinction between a valid argument and a sound one: an argument is sound only if it is valid ``and has no false premises'' (Wikipedia, ``Soundness''). Validity alone holds in every world, including those without Socrates.}

\cpara{The step from validity to evidence, and it is correct. Evidence favors a hypothesis when it is likelier if the hypothesis is true than if it is false; a fact that holds either way favors neither.}
\cpara{Restates the previous paragraph in terms of possible worlds.}
\cpara{Limits the claim: logic can tell us what we do not yet know follows from what we already accept.}
\cpara{Applies this to Socrates: logic shows what two uncertain guesses predict together.}

\cpara{The suggestion is not credited. The phrase comes from the title of a 1975 paper by Jaakko Hintikka, ``Impossible Possible Worlds Vindicated'' (\textsc{Journal of Philosophical Logic}); the \textsc{Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy} (``Impossible Worlds'') describes admitting impossible worlds into models of knowledge, so that a person need not know every logical truth, as a popular method, ``beginning with Cresswell 1973 and Hintikka 1975.''}
\cpara{Keeps empirical predictions apart from that kind of logical learning.}
\cpara{The conclusion, consistent with the concessions before it: logic connects hypotheses to observations and predictions, and settles no empirical question by itself.}
\cpara{Closes with a two-line verse that restates the thesis.}
